Alex 1

Putting a short write-up and an example workbook on this thread. Attachment: velocity_pricing_model.xlsx (tabbed: assumptions / marginal_vs_blend / monthly_trueup). High level:

1) Velocity-based crediting concept:
   - Instead of fixed slab breakpoints (e.g., 0-1B @ $0.012, 1B-3B @ $0.009), we apply a dynamic per-token credit that scales with your 7-day moving token velocity. When velocity crosses thresholds, the credit for subsequent tokens changes (marginal), but we also support a blended invoice option for customers that prefer a single effective rate.

2) Marginal vs blended:
   - Marginal: tokens are billed at the rate for the bucket they fall into during the billing window. Good for customers with predictable spikes who want the lowest cost for additional tokens.
   - Blended: at month-end we compute (total spend / total tokens) and invoice a single effective $/token. This reduces invoice volatility for both sides.

3) True-up & credits:
   - We do a month-close reconciliation. If velocity downgrades mid-month and you had received higher credits, the reconciliation will bill the delta (or apply a credit if velocity increased). We cap retroactive clawbacks to the monthly commit (see term sheet).

4) Minimums & overages:
   - Typical starter commitment: 1.5B tokens/mo minimum for reserved discount tier; overages billed at capped rate (we can set a hard cap so you never pay more than X per token on overages).

I've sketched two illustrative scenarios in the workbook using your 4B average / 1.6B peak numbers. Quick ask: are you comfortable with a month-end blended invoice (simpler) or do you prefer pure marginal billing (potentially optimal $ but more variable)?

If helpful, happy to jump on a 30-min call with your procurement and finance to walk the workbook.

Alex 1

Looping in a couple of concrete examples and the legal-safe phrasing for the cap. Below are two short scenarios pulled from the workbook; I flattened the math so you can paste into your model.

Scenario A (marginal behavior 1 no retroactive reprice):
- Assumptions: base tier 0-1B @ $0.012, next tier 1B-3B @ $0.009, next tier 3B-6B @ $0.007. Velocity thresholds defined by 7-day moving average.
- Month day 1-14: 2B tokens (billed 1B at $0.012 + 1B at $0.009)
- Day 15-30 spike: +3B tokens (these fall into 3B-6B tier and are billed at $0.007 marginally)
- Result: earlier tokens keep their paid rate; spike tokens get marginal lower rate. Effective blended rate = (compute total spend / total tokens) but invoice line items show marginal charges.

Scenario B (blended month-end single rate with smoothing):
- Compute raw effective rate = total_spend / total_tokens.
- Smoothing: customers can elect a 48-hour burst exclusion window for a single month once per quarter; that window excludes tokens from blended calc and instead invoices them at the overage cap rate. This helps with big one-off reprocesses.

Clawback cap language (legal-safe):
"Customer acknowledges that Redwood may perform monthly reconciliations of billed credits. Any retroactive adjustments that increase Customer liability will be capped at the committed monthly token quantity (the "Commit"). Excess retroactive charges beyond the Commit will be waived. Adjustments that reduce Customer liability will be issued as a credit to the subsequent invoice."

Additional behavioral note: velocity-based crediting is a middle ground 1 it prevents a one-day spike from downgrading your whole-month effective rate (because crediting follows a moving average) while still letting you get better marginal economics during sustained high-throughput periods. Slab is simpler but can over-penalize short bursts.

Attachment: term_sheet_v2.pdf has the same clause in section 4.2.

If procurement wants, I can produce a 12-month cashflow illustration with several burst patterns.

1Marissa
